newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenian stock exchange to launch new share index.
newsitem.headline: Slovenian stock exchange to launch new share index.

text.p: The Ljubljana Stock Exchange said on Wednesday it would launch a new blue-chip index at the start of next year in an effort to create a more representative share basket and lure new investors to the fledgling market.

The new index, which should start trading in January, will replace the existing seven share SBI index. The SBI has recently come under fire from investors, who argue that sharp price movements in individual shares can throw the whole market out of kilter.

"In the new year we will adopt a completely new index that will be weighted to represent market capitalisation and will include new companies," bourse president Drasko Veselinovic told Reuters in an interview.

He said about 10 shares would make up the index, which should pass muster with international stock exchanges. Participating shares would have to reach minimum standards for market capitalisation and liquidity, he said.
Details will be announced in December.
Veselinovic defended the two-year record of the old SBI index but conceded that problems at some high-profile listed companies this year had undermined investor confidence.

Shares in financial consultancy Dadas, for example, have plummeted 90 percent since the end of March when Slovenia's securities watchdog started proceedings to ban Dadas' brokerage arm from trading. Dadas' woes affected the whole SBI index.

"We are aware of the shortcomings of this index but we couldn't have done any better than we did at the time," Veselinovic said, noting that when the stock exchange first compiled the SBI it had very few companies to choose from.
"Dadas is one episode we cannot deny...but I would say it is not in focus any more."
Veselinovic said he was pinning his hopes for greater liquidity on the arrival of newly privatised companies.
So far this year shares in 27 formerly state owned firms have begun trading -- seven of them on the primary market.

In September foreign investors began putting money into debutantes like pharmaceutical company Lek and food producers Droga and Kolinska. Their involvement has helped boost average daily turnover by around 70 percent since mid-September.

Slovenia's only port Luka Koper, mineral water producer Radenska, tyre producer Sava and petrol trading company Istrabenz can expect to draw similar investor interest when they enter the market, according to Veselinovic.
The stock exchange chief brushed aside speculation that the central bank may soon act to stem the inflow of foreign capital.
The central bank jealously guards the amount of foreign currency in circulation as part of its strategy to maintain the stability of the tolar.
"The Bank of Slovenia has said it is monitoring the matter but does not intend to do anything so far," Veselinovic said.
He also insisted that existing legislation governing foreign portfolio investments did not discourage outsiders from entering the Slovenian market.
Nevertheless, he forecast the government would liberalise the rules early next year.

"The point is that current legislation is not prohibiting foreign investments," Veselinovic said. "(But) the new law, which has been prepared already, is very liberal and I expect this law to enter the parliamentary procedure in the spring."
